content: 1. Stefano Vella, affiliated with Istituto Superiore di Sanità in Italy, declared no conflicts of interest at the start of the Clinical Guideline Development Group meeting in June 2015. No conflicts were identified or disclosed. 2. Jared Baeten, from the University of Washington, United States, received grant support exceeding $70 million from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, the United States National Institutes of Health (NIH), and USAID for research related to pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). Additionally, Gilead Sciences donated PrEP medication to his research unit without providing other monetary support. These financial interests were deemed significant. 3. Suna Balkan, representing Médecins Sans Frontières in France, declared no conflicts of interest. 4. Carlos Cáceres, from Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia in Peru, coordinates a network for multidisciplinary studies on antiretroviral-based HIV prevention. This network has received support from WHO and UNAIDS but does not promote any specific product. The financial interests were considered non-significant. 5. Frank Chimbwandira, from the Ministry of Health in Malawi, declared no conflicts of interest. 6. Simon Collins, affiliated with HIV i-Base in the United Kingdom, declared no conflicts of interest. 7. Frances Cowan, from University College London and CeSHHAR Zimbabwe, is the principal investigator for a trial on antiretroviral therapy (ART) as prevention among female sex workers in Zimbabwe. Gilead donated drugs for PrEP to this trial. These non-monetary contributions were considered non-significant. 8. Mitzy Gafos, from University College London, declared no conflicts of interest. 9. Alison Grant, from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, declared no conflicts of interest. 10. Juan Vicente Guanira, from Investigaciones Médicas en Salud in Argentina, declared no conflicts of interest. 11. Jessica Haberer, from Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard University, United States, conducted consulting work for FHI 360 ($500), WHO on PrEP adherence ($9,900), and the NIH on behavioral science ($6,700 annually). She also received research support from the NIH and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, including salary support, as a principal and co-investigator. These financial interests were deemed significant. 12. Hakima Himmi, from Association Lutte Contre le Sida in Morocco, declared no conflicts of interest. 13. Rohan Hazra, from the NIH and the United States Department of Health and Human Services, declared no conflicts of interest. 14. Sarah Huffam, from the National Centre for HIV/AIDS, Dermatology, and STIs in Cambodia, was employed as a consultant to write the Cambodian national HIV management guidelines. This financial interest was deemed significant. 15. Jonathan Kaplan, from the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, declared no conflicts of interest. 16. Valdilea Goncalves Veloso, from the Oswaldo Cruz Foundation in Brazil, declared no conflicts of interest. 17. Iryna Zablotska, from the Kirby Institute in Australia, received research support from Gilead (A$40,000) and medication supply for a PrEP demonstration study (PRELUDE). These financial interests were deemed significant. 18. Vincent Wong, from USAID in the United States, had travel expenses paid by his employer, USAID. This financial interest was considered non-significant. 19. Anton Pozniak, from Chelsea and Westminster NHS Foundation Trust in the United Kingdom, conducted research into drugs through his institution and attended pharmaceutical-sponsored meetings and travel funded by ViiV Healthcare, Merck, BMS, Gilead, and Janssen. He is also a member of the BHIVA and EACS guidelines committees. These financial interests were deemed significant. 20. Gayle Sherman, from the University of Witwatersrand in South Africa, declared no conflicts of interest. 21. Kwasi Torpey, from Family Health International (FHI 360) in Nigeria, declared no conflicts of interest.
